doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Hearing Elvin Jones in Amsterdam, and Al Levitt
summary: He hears Elvin Jones in Amsterdam in 1957 after Al Levitt describes him; later they live near each other in New York.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I met Elvin when he worked with J.J. Johnson’s quintet with Tommy Flanagan, Wilbur Little and Bobby Jaspar, the Belgian saxophonist, in Amsterdam. I had heard about him through Al Levitt, the late Al Levitt, the drummer who was from New York and played with Lenny Tristano and Stan Getz and Lee Konitz and well quite a few other people. I had heard of Al through reading about his name in Down Beat, on records. And he was in Holland the first time I went to Europe, working with Pia Beck, the Dutch pianist, who had enjoyed some popularity in the middle and late 50s, and she worked the summer at a club outside of the Hague, at a resort called Skathagian. And these guys I was there with, a college Dixieland band, somehow wrangled a booking playing the intermissions opposite Pia Beck and I got to know Al Levitt there, we became fast friends. And I think he was really the one who first told me about Elvin. He tried to describe Elvin’s playing to me. He said, “It sounds like all these little explosions.” It didn’t mean anything to me. And then the next summer I took my own band to Europe and I don’t remember how we got hooked up but we ended up opening this concert at the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam for J.J.’s quintet. And Elvin was the drummer. And that’s where I first heard him and met him. And after the concert we all retired to the Scheherazade Club, which was THE jazz club in Amsterdam at the time, and some of us sat in. And Elvin sat in. And I couldn’t believe what I was hearing man. It sounded completely different than anything I had heard before by a jazz drummer. It just triggered all kinds of things in my imagination. It sounded like slow motion. It was like nothing I ever heard before.

Yeah I liked it, yeah I definitely liked it. I was impressed. It was like revolutionary. It seems like — well I’ve read Elvin played polyrhythms, one rhythm against another rhythm and so forth, and it did kind of sound like that actually. At the same time it still was rooted in the tradition of Max Roach, Art Blakey, Jo Jones and so forth. But it was like nothing I had ever heard before. It was kind of revolutionary to me. He seemed to incorporate all the drums more than anybody had before into his total persona. You didn’t just hear the cymbal, you heard everything — it was like ten different things going on at once. And he didn’t know me. I guess maybe he heard me play before, I don’t know, maybe he was in the dressing room. We spoke and, but then I got to New York, let’s see, well actually it was that fall. That was in the summer of ’57. In October of ’57 I moved to New York. And I don’t think I saw much of Elvin until I moved to the lower east side in January of ’59 I think it was. And Elvin just so happened to have the same landlord as I did but in a building a block away from me. And I think he came in the Five Spot while I was working there. He was still working with J.J. I think. And the next thing I know he just started asking me — he started sending me on subs.
